section_summary: This section covers Department of State records from July 1940 to June 1944 relating to Japanese nationality and the citizenship status of Japanese-Americans. It documents efforts by American citizens of Japanese descent, particularly in Hawaii and internment camps, to expatriate from Japan or renounce dual nationality under Japanese nationality laws and the U.S. Nationality Act of 1940. The records also include legal memoranda, congressional inquiries, and public correspondence analyzing birthright citizenship under the Fourteenth Amendment, Japanese legal codes governing military obligation and family registry, and the availability of expatriation statistics.

subfiles.about: Consulate in Kobe requests instructions regarding the citizenship status of dual citizen Tadayoshi Kondo after his father reinstated him in the Japanese family record.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference sheet indexing Despatch No. 304-305 from the American Consulate in Kobe, dated July 13, 1940. The despatch requests instructions regarding the citizenship status of Tadayoshi Kondo, a person of dual nationality whose father had him reinstated in the Japanese family record (koseki) after he reached majority under Japanese law. The original paper is filed under 130-Kondo, Tadayoshi (894.012/35).
subfiles.title: Citizenship Status of Tadayoshi Kondo

subfiles.about: Department of State informs Radford Mobley that procedures for divesting Japanese nationality fall within the jurisdiction of the Japanese government.
subfiles.from: Department of State (Division of Far Eastern Affairs)
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference sheet indexing a letter dated November 16, 1940 to Radford Mobley of the Washington Press Service. The letter explains that facilitating procedures for persons of Japanese race in Hawaii who hold American nationality to divest themselves of Japanese nationality lies within the jurisdiction of the foreign government concerned. It notes that the Division of Far Eastern Affairs is prepared to discuss the matter if further assistance is desired. The original paper is filed under 130 Japanese/86 (894.012/36).
subfiles.title: Procedure for Divestment of Japanese Nationality in Hawaii

subfiles.about: Hawaiian Sugar Planters Association prepares a petition urging the State Department to arrange simplified expatriation procedures with Japan.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference sheet indexing correspondence from the Hawaiian Sugar Planters Association in Honolulu, dated December 10, 1940. The association requests a simplified procedure allowing American citizens of Japanese ancestry, particularly in Hawaii, to expatriate from Japanese nationality. It indicates that a petition is being prepared for presentation to the State Department to exercise its authority with the Government of Japan to facilitate such arrangements. The original paper is filed under 130-Japanese/80 (894.012/37).
subfiles.title: Petition for Simplified Expatriation Procedure in Hawaii

subfiles.about: American Consulate at Nagasaki transmits statistical background data on the application of nationality legislation to registered Americans of Japanese race.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference sheet indexing Despatch No. 255 from Consul Arthur H. Tower at Nagasaki, dated January 17, 1941. The despatch furnishes statistical background data relating to the application of recent nationality legislation to registered Americans of Japanese race residing within the consular district. The original paper is filed under 130 Japanese/106 (894.012/38).
subfiles.title: Statistical Data on Registered Americans of Japanese Race in Nagasaki

subfiles.about: Embassy in Tokyo forwards a summary of Japanese press reports on how the new Nationality Act affects Nisei in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference sheet indexing Despatch No. 5304 from Ambassador Joseph C. Grew in Tokyo, dated January 21, 1941. The despatch summarizes an article from the Japan Times and Advertiser of January 13, 1941 (translated from Miyako of January 12) entitled 'New American Law Puzzles Nisei Here.' The article reports that American citizens of Japanese race residing in Japan who fail to return to the United States between January 13 and July 14 will lose American citizenship under the Nationality Act of 1940. The original paper is filed under 136(1940)/25 (894.012/39).
subfiles.title: Japanese Press Coverage of the Nationality Act of 1940

subfiles.about: Allen Douglas advises on Japanese-American renunciation of Japanese nationality and opposes Hawaiian statehood due to the Japanese majority.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference sheet indexing correspondence from Allen Douglas, dated January 26, 1941. The writer advocates an easy method to permit Japanese-Americans to renounce Japanese nationality, asserts that local Japanese remain loyal to the Japanese Emperor, and argues that Hawaii should no longer be called the Hawaiian Islands. He also warns against granting statehood to Hawaii in light of the Japanese population majority. The original paper is filed under 130 Japanese/101 (894.012/40).
subfiles.title: Renunciation of Japanese Nationality and Opposition to Hawaiian Statehood

subfiles.about: Delegate Samuel W. King requests permission to present a petition on behalf of Hawaiian citizens of Japanese ancestry regarding expatriation.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference sheet indexing correspondence dated January 27, 1941 from Samuel W. King, Delegate to Congress from Hawaii. King asserts that renunciation by American citizens of Japanese ancestry residing in Hawaii is completely within the control of the United States Government. He requests permission to present a petition to the State Department in connection with the matter. The original paper is filed under 130 Japanese/102 (894.012/41).
subfiles.title: Request by Delegate Samuel W. King to Present Expatriation Petition

subfiles.about: Consulate at Osaka reports that William Merrell Vories renounced American citizenship after being adopted into his Japanese wife's family.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference sheet indexing Despatch No. 166 from Consul John M. Allison at Osaka, dated January 31, 1941. The despatch reports the renunciation of American citizenship by William Merrell Vories, who acquired Japanese nationality by adoption into the family of his Japanese wife pursuant to Japanese law and assumed her family name, Hitotsuyanagi. The original paper is filed under 130-Vories, William Merrell (894.012/42).
subfiles.title: Renunciation of American Citizenship by William Merrell Vories

subfiles.about: American Loyalty League of Fresno inquires how to demonstrate Nisei loyalty and urges legislation ending dual nationality.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference sheet indexing correspondence dated March 31, 1941 from the American Loyalty League of Fresno, California. The organization inquires how the American public can be made aware of the sincere allegiance of Japanese-American citizens to the United States. It further urges the enactment of legislation to eliminate dual citizenship and prevent foreign governments from asserting claims over dual nationals. The original paper is filed under 130-Japanese/113 (894.012/43).
subfiles.title: Inquiry by American Loyalty League on Allegiance and Dual Citizenship

subfiles.about: Consulate at Osaka transmits a letter from Naoki Nishiyama expressing loyalty to Japan as typical of Japan-educated Nisei.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference sheet indexing Despatch No. 44 from Consul John M. Allison at Osaka, dated December 13, 1940. The despatch transmits a letter from Naoki Nishiyama expressing loyalty to Japan rather than the United States, which the consul characterizes as typical of American-born Japanese educated in Japan (Kibei). The original paper is filed under 130 Japanese/97 (894.012/44).
subfiles.title: Letter of Naoki Nishiyama Regarding Loyalty of Japan-Educated Nisei

subfiles.about: Embassy in Tokyo reports inquiries by Japanese-Americans in Japan regarding expatriation under Section 402 of the Nationality Act of 1940.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference sheet indexing Telegram No. 137 from Ambassador Joseph C. Grew at Tokyo, dated January 20, 1941. The telegram relays inquiries from American citizens of Japanese race residing in Japan as to whether they will be deemed expatriated at the end of the six-month statutory period under Section 402 of the Nationality Act of 1940, noting that their Japanese passports have expired and estimating that approximately 4,000 Japanese-Americans are affected. The original paper is filed under 130(1940)/56 (894.012/45).
subfiles.title: Status of Japanese-Americans in Japan under Section 402 of Nationality Act

subfiles.about: State Department memorandum analyzes conflicting estimates of dual citizens in Hawaii seeking expatriation from Japan.
subfiles.from: Department of State (Division of Far Eastern Affairs - Herbert P. Fales)
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference sheet indexing an internal memorandum dated April 10, 1941 prepared by Herbert P. Fales of the Division of Far Eastern Affairs. The memorandum addresses the number of Japanese dual citizens in Hawaii allegedly seeking expatriation from Japan. It notes reports from the War Department (Hawaiian Department) that misleading statements are circulating, compares Professor Shunzo Sakamaki's estimate of 1,600 with the Territorial Bureau of Vital Statistics figure of 3,500, and cites Japanese Consulate General reports of 1,700 applicants in 1940 compared to 1,527 in 1939. The original paper is filed under 134 Hawaii/360 (894.012/46).
subfiles.title: Estimates of Japanese Dual Citizens in Hawaii Seeking Expatriation

subfiles.about: Department of the Interior forwards a petition signed by over 30,000 Hawaiian citizens of Japanese ancestry requesting simplified expatriation.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference sheet indexing a letter dated April 29, 1941 from the Department of the Interior. The letter forwards a petition signed by over 30,000 American citizens of Japanese ancestry residing in Hawaii requesting the good offices of the State Department to negotiate with the Japanese Government to simplify existing expatriation procedures. The petition was transmitted through Delegate Samuel W. King along with letters from the Governor of Hawaii, territorial officials, and civic leaders. The original paper is filed under 130 Japanese/117 (894.012/47).
subfiles.title: Transmittal of Hawaii Expatriation Petition by Department of the Interior

subfiles.about: Senate of Hawaii transmits Senate Concurrent Resolution No. 35 requesting State Department assistance to simplify Japanese expatriation.
subfiles.from: Senate of the Territory of Hawaii
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference sheet indexing a letter dated April 30, 1941 from the Senate of the Territory of Hawaii. The letter transmits a certified copy of Senate Concurrent Resolution No. 35, adopted April 24, 1941, memorializing the Department of State to exercise its good offices to secure a simplified procedure for expatriation from Japanese nationality. The original paper is filed under 130 Japanese/122 (894.012/48).
subfiles.title: Hawaii Senate Concurrent Resolution No. 35 on Expatriation Procedure

subfiles.about: Japanese American Citizens League of San Diego forwards resolutions pledging allegiance to the United States and renouncing Japanese rights.
subfiles.from: Japanese American Citizens League of San Diego (Otsuka)
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference sheet indexing a letter dated January 24, 1942 from the Japanese American Citizens League of San Diego, California (transmitted by Otsuka). The letter encloses resolutions unanimously adopted at a regular meeting wherein league members pledge allegiance to the United States and formally denounce and repudiate all rights and allegiances under the laws of the Japanese Empire. The original paper is filed under 130 Japanese/159 (894.012/49).
subfiles.title: Resolutions of the Japanese American Citizens League of San Diego

subfiles.about: U.S. censorship officers intercept and condemn two expatriation applications from Hawaiian residents addressed to the Japanese Consulate General.
subfiles.summary: Office of Censorship interception report (Records No. NY 5309-42) regarding a condemned letter postmarked December 3, 1941 from Shigeko Asato in Pepeekeo, Hawaii, addressed to the Japanese Consulate General in Honolulu. The examiners note that the envelope contained two applications by Hawaiian residents for expatriation from Japan, accompanied by a certificate of approval for Shigeko Asato, family records (koseki), and a letter from the Secretary of Hawaii. The report contains administrative routing stamps, inter-agency distribution markings, and examiner determinations completed between March 2 and March 25, 1942 under decimal 894.012/50.
subfiles.title: Censorship Record NY 5309-42: Expatriation Applications of Shigeko Asato

subfiles.about: Representative Francis Case inquires into the dual citizenship and expatriation status of Lillian Higashi through the Chicago Consulate.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference sheet indexing a letter dated April 2, 1942 to Representative Francis Case concerning an inquiry on behalf of Lillian Higashi. Higashi sought advice regarding her dual citizenship status, uncertain whether her expatriation documents had been finalized through the Japanese Consulate in Chicago prior to the outbreak of war. The original paper is filed under 130-Higashi, Lillian (894.012/51).
subfiles.title: Expatriation Status of Lillian Higashi

subfiles.about: Flournoy discusses Senator Stewart's proposed legislation to strip Japanese-Americans of citizenship and potential reversal of Wong Kim Ark.
subfiles.from: Department of State Legal Adviser (Richard W. Flournoy)
keywords: United States v. Wong Kim Ark
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference sheet indexing correspondence dated February 11, 1942 from Richard W. Flournoy to the Legal Adviser. The document discusses Senator Tom Stewart's interest in legislation to deprive American-born Japanese of U.S. citizenship. It specifically analyzes whether it would be possible to obtain a Supreme Court decision reversing the landmark 1898 precedent in United States v. Wong Kim Ark. The original paper is filed under 130 Japanese/167 (894.012/51-1/2).
subfiles.title: Senator Stewart's Proposal on Expatriating American-Born Japanese

subfiles.about: Embassy in Tokyo forwards a magazine article by Professor Takizo Matsumoto analyzing the second-generation Japanese problem.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference sheet indexing a despatch dated April 6, 1942 from Ambassador Joseph C. Grew in Tokyo. The despatch transmits a clipping of a magazine article regarding second-generation Japanese written by Professor Takizo Matsumoto of Meiji University. The report notes that although Matsumoto is not himself a Nisei, he was educated in the United States and has long been active in second-generation affairs in both countries. The original paper is filed under 894.00/1158 (894.012/52-1/2).
subfiles.title: Magazine Article by Professor Takizo Matsumoto on Second-Generation Japanese

subfiles.about: War Relocation Authority submits evacuee statements expressing dual citizenship and seeking renunciation of American citizenship.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference sheet indexing an undated submission from the War Relocation Authority. The submission transmits copies of statements made by Japanese evacuees indicating that they possess dual citizenship and desire to renounce their American citizenship, submitted to the Department of State for verification. The original paper is filed under 130 Japanese/183 (894.012/53).
subfiles.title: War Relocation Authority Submissions on Evacuee Renunciation Statements

subfiles.about: State Department issues instructions to the Legation in Bern regarding acquisition of Japanese nationality by Frank Quini and siblings.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference sheet indexing an instruction dated August 24, 1943 from Charles E. Tait of the Department of State to the American Legation in Bern, Switzerland. The instruction concerns American interests in Japan and the citizenship status of Frank Quini and his siblings, transmitting translations relative to their acquisition of Japanese nationality. The original paper is filed under 130-Quini, Frank (894.012/54).
subfiles.title: Instruction to Bern Regarding Citizenship of Frank Quini

subfiles.about: Legation in Bern transmits affidavit and baptismal certificate seeking repatriation exchange inclusion for Emilia Quini.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference sheet indexing Despatch No. 5970 dated August 25, 1943 from the American Legation in Bern (Charles E. Tait). The despatch transmits an affidavit to overcome the presumption of expatriation and a copy of a baptismal certificate in connection with residence and employment in Japan for Emilia Quini. The Legation requests that the case be re-examined to permit inclusion in an upcoming diplomatic exchange due to precarious financial circumstances and the desire to provide an American education for her daughter. The original paper is filed under 130-Quini, Emilia (894.012/55).
subfiles.title: Despatch from Bern Regarding Repatriation Exchange of Emilia Quini

subfiles.about: State Department informs Spanish Embassy that U.S. citizens interned at Gila River cannot legally renounce U.S. citizenship while in the country.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference sheet indexing a memorandum dated March 8, 1943 to the Spanish Embassy regarding the abandonment of American citizenship by Japanese nationals interned at the Gila Relocation Center in Rivers, Arizona. The Department advises that under Sections 403(a) and 408 of the Nationality Act of 1940, there is no statutory procedure by which American citizens residing within the United States may renounce their nationality or divest themselves of American citizenship. The original paper is filed under 136(1940)/668 (894.012/56).
subfiles.title: Memorandum on Inability of Gila River Internees to Renounce Citizenship

subfiles.about: Flournoy advises Passport Division that dual national children lose Japanese nationality unless registered at a consulate within two weeks of birth.
subfiles.from: Department of State Legal Adviser (Richard W. Flournoy)
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference sheet indexing a memorandum dated March 26, 1943 from Richard W. Flournoy to the Passport Division regarding the status under Japanese law of children born in the United States to Japanese parents. Flournoy clarifies that Article 20(2), enacted by the amendment effective December 1, 1924, is treated by Japanese authorities as a separate article; under its terms, any child born in the United States who acquires Japanese nationality at birth forfeits it retroactively unless registered at a Japanese consulate within two weeks. The original paper is filed under 130 Japanese/122 (894.012/57).
subfiles.title: Memorandum on Consular Registration under Article 20(2) of Japanese Law

subfiles.about: Vincent Cope argues that American-born Japanese are not U.S. citizens because dual nationality excludes them from U.S. jurisdiction.
subfiles.summary: Letter dated November 30, 1943 from Vincent Cope of Fort Lupton, Colorado to the Secretary of State. Cope presents a detailed legal argument contending that the Fourteenth Amendment does not confer citizenship on American-born Japanese because their dual allegiance under Japanese law prevents them from being 'subject to the jurisdiction' of the United States. He quotes Article 24 of the Japanese Nationality Law, arguing that a Japanese male cannot dissolve his military obligations to the Emperor before death, and asserts that immigration authorities' acquiescence to passport-free travel does not estop the government from denying their citizenship. He further contends that Japanese residents constitute an unassimilated minority maintaining Japanese customs and schools, drawing legal analogies to non-citizen tribal Indians under Elk v. Wilkins and unincorporated territorial inhabitants under Gonzales v. Williams.
subfiles.title: Letter from Vincent Cope Challenging Citizenship of American-Born Japanese

subfiles.about: Office of Coordination and Review suggests that Legal Adviser Hackworth sign the reply to Vincent Cope.
subfiles.from: Department of State (Office of Coordination and Review - C. R. Rockwell)
subfiles.summary: Routing slip dated December 29, 1943 from C. R. Rockwell of the Office of Coordination and Review to the Legal Adviser's office. Rockwell recommends that the Department's response to Vincent Cope be prepared for the signature of Legal Adviser Green H. Hackworth rather than an Assistant Secretary. He requests that changes be marked directly on the blue draft copy to obviate the need for re-initialing by reviewing officers.
subfiles.title: Routing Slip Regarding Draft Reply to Vincent Cope
subfiles.to: Department of State Legal Adviser (Green H. Hackworth)

subfiles.about: Flournoy analyzes Vincent Cope's letter, noting contrasting loyalty between Nisei soldiers and Japan-educated Kibei.
subfiles.from: Department of State Legal Adviser (Richard W. Flournoy)
subfiles.summary: Internal memorandum dated December 22, 1943 from Richard W. Flournoy to Green H. Hackworth, Laurence Salisbury, and Joseph W. Ballantine concerning persons born in the United States to Japanese parents. Flournoy observes that Vincent Cope's letter reflects a practical grasp of dual nationality problems despite the author's apparent youth. He points out that while thousands of Nisei serving in the U.S. armed forces are entirely loyal, reports from diplomatic and consular posts confirm that American-born Japanese sent to Japan as minors for education (Kibei) are predominantly loyal to Japan. He concludes that an extended debate with Cope is undesirable and advises against discussing pre-war travel practices in the official reply.
subfiles.title: Memorandum on Vincent Cope Letter and Loyalty of Dual Nationals
subfiles.to: Green H. Hackworth, Laurence Salisbury, and Joseph W. Ballantine

subfiles.about: State Department provides Vincent Cope with legal citations on the citizenship status of children born to alien parents.
subfiles.from: Department of State Legal Adviser (Green H. Hackworth)
keywords: United States v. Wong Kim Ark
subfiles.summary: Official carbon copy and preliminary blue draft of a letter dated January 3, 1944 from Legal Adviser Green H. Hackworth to Vincent Cope in Fort Lupton, Colorado. Responding to Cope's inquiry of November 30, 1943 concerning the citizenship and loyalty of children of Japanese parents, Hackworth refers him to leading legal authorities on the status of persons born in the United States to alien parents. The citations include the Supreme Court decision in United States v. Wong Kim Ark, Frederick Van Dyne's Citizenship of the United States, John Bassett Moore's Digest of International Law, and Hackworth's own Digest of International Law. The subfile includes the final letter copy and the marked-up draft sheet reflecting coordination revisions.
subfiles.title: Letter to Vincent Cope Citing Authorities on Birthright Citizenship

subfiles.about: Flournoy advises Hackworth that Japanese law does not permit persons of Japanese descent to acquire Japanese nationality while in the U.S.
subfiles.from: Department of State Legal Adviser (Richard W. Flournoy)
subfiles.summary: Two-page memorandum dated November 23, 1943 from Richard W. Flournoy to Legal Adviser Green H. Hackworth regarding whether persons of Japanese descent born in the United States can acquire Japanese nationality while in the country. Prompted by a telephone inquiry from Representative Bertrand W. Gearhart, Flournoy examines the Japanese Nationality Law of 1899, the 1916 and 1924 amendments, and Ordinance No. 26, finding that naturalization generally requires domicile in Japan except under Article 11 for meritorious services. He discusses consultations with Paul L. Johansen (FE) and Albert E. Clattenburg Jr. (Special Division), noting that cases heard by Gearhart likely involve Japanese nationals renewing passports through the Spanish Embassy or disloyal evacuees transferred to Tule Lake seeking repatriation to Japan.
subfiles.title: Memorandum on Acquisition of Japanese Nationality While in the United States

subfiles.about: State Department discusses policy regarding the departure and exchange of individuals possessing dual U.S. and Japanese nationality.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference sheet indexing a communication dated April 30, 1943 to the Spanish Embassy regarding the attitude of the United States Government toward the departure from the United States in connection with diplomatic exchanges of persons possessing both American and Japanese nationality. The original paper is filed under 311.9416/560 (894.012/60).
subfiles.title: U.S. Policy Regarding Exchange of Dual U.S.-Japanese Nationals

subfiles.about: State Department transmits a five-page memorandum quoting Japanese nationality laws and ordinances to Representative Bertrand W. Gearhart.
subfiles.from: Department of State Legal Adviser (Green H. Hackworth)
subfiles.summary: Letter dated November 23, 1943 from Legal Adviser Green H. Hackworth to Representative Bertrand W. Gearhart, transmitting a comprehensive five-page memorandum on Japanese nationality legislation. The memorandum provides English translations of Articles 1, 7, 11, 20(2), 24, and 25-27 of Law No. 66 of 1899 as revised in 1916 and 1924, outlining rules governing jus sanguinis paternity, naturalization domicile conditions, retroactive forfeiture of Japanese nationality for children born in designated foreign countries (including the U.S.), and military service exceptions under Article 24 preventing males 17 and older from losing nationality without completing active duty. It also incorporates Imperial Ordinance No. 26 of November 17, 1924 detailing procedural regulations for birth reports, renunciation through Japanese diplomatic missions, and recovery of nationality. The subfile includes the transmittal letter, the original memorandum, and three identical carbon copies preserved in State Department records.
subfiles.title: Letter and Memorandum for Representative Bertrand W. Gearhart on Japanese Nationality Laws

subfiles.about: Vincent Cope argues that Selective Service 4-C draft status and Japanese religious beliefs demonstrate that Nisei are foreign subjects.
subfiles.summary: Letter dated January 27, 1944 from Vincent Cope in Fort Lupton, Colorado to the Secretary of State submitting further arguments against birthright citizenship for American-born Japanese. Cope cites their Selective Service draft classification in Class 4-C as proof of alien status and argues that under Ex parte McCardle jurisdiction means 'the power to declare law,' which Japan exercised through its 1899 nationality law and comity. He contends that Section 2 of Article 20 designates dual nationals as 'Japanese subjects' who can only acquire American nationality through affirmative congressional naturalization acts, which are legally blocked for males over 17 by Article 24 absent a treaty. He concludes by questioning whether allegiance to the Emperor through Buddhist and Shinto ancestor worship is compatible with loyalty to the United States.
subfiles.title: Letter from Vincent Cope on Selective Service Status and Japanese Nationality Laws

subfiles.about: State Department declines to express an official legal opinion on Vincent Cope's theoretical citizenship arguments.
subfiles.from: Department of State Legal Adviser (Green H. Hackworth)
subfiles.summary: Official letter dated February 9, 1944 from Legal Adviser Green H. Hackworth to Vincent Cope in Fort Lupton, Colorado. Hackworth acknowledges Cope's letter of January 27 regarding the status of persons born in the United States to Japanese parents. He informs Cope that while his views have been noted with interest, the Department cannot consistently with its established practice express an official opinion because Cope has not presented a specific case requiring Department action.
subfiles.title: Letter to Vincent Cope Declining to Render Legal Opinion

subfiles.about: Vincent Cope forwards to Secretary Cordell Hull a copy of his letter to Attorney General Biddle arguing that Nisei are enemy aliens.
subfiles.summary: Transmittal letter dated June 16, 1944 from Vincent Cope to Secretary of State Cordell Hull enclosing a copy of his letter sent on June 15, 1944 to Attorney General Francis Biddle. In the enclosed communication to Biddle, Cope argues that the concept of dual citizenship for American-born Japanese is legally erroneous and that under the rule of jus sanguinis recognized by the United States, they are exclusively Japanese subjects not subject to U.S. jurisdiction under the Fourteenth Amendment. He asserts that Congress possesses plenary constitutional authority over naturalization, meaning persons of Japanese descent born in the United States remain enemy aliens unless naturalized by federal statute. Citing Ex parte McCardle, South Carolina v. United States, McCulloch v. Maryland, Oceanic Navigation Co. v. Stranahan, and Hall's International Law, he maintains that while Japanese aliens may be compelled to perform emergency military defense against invasion, administrative agencies and courts lack constitutional authority to treat them as citizens.
subfiles.title: Letter from Vincent Cope to Cordell Hull Transmitting Letter to Attorney General Biddle

subfiles.about: State Department transmits a memorandum to Representative Clarence E. Hancock regarding acquisition of Chinese or Japanese nationality.
subfiles.summary: Letter dated October 28, 1943 from the Department of State to Representative Clarence E. Hancock of New York following up on a conversation regarding the possibility of American citizens acquiring Chinese or Japanese nationality. The writer transmits a memorandum prepared by a Department official (Swanson) who specialized in the question, apologizing for the delay in forwarding the information and expressing hope that it will prove useful to the Congressman.
subfiles.title: Letter to Representative Clarence E. Hancock on Acquiring Chinese or Japanese Nationality

subfiles.about: L. Curtis Guise requests official statistics on American-born Japanese who expatriated under Japanese nationality laws.
subfiles.summary: Letter dated June 13, 1944 from L. Curtis Guise in Claremont, California to Joseph C. Grew, Director of the Office of Far Eastern Affairs. Guise explains that he is preparing a research paper on Japanese-American relations and seeks reliable statistical information regarding the extent to which American-born Japanese availed themselves of the expatriation provisions in the Japanese Nationality Laws of March 1916 and July 1924. While acknowledging that Japanese consular archives are the property of Japan, he asks whether any authoritative figures have been released.
subfiles.title: Inquiry by L. Curtis Guise Regarding Expatriation Statistics

subfiles.about: Joseph C. Grew informs L. Curtis Guise that the State Department has no statistics on Japanese expatriation by Nisei.
subfiles.from: Department of State (Office of Far Eastern Affairs - Joseph C. Grew)
subfiles.summary: Official letter dated June 27, 1944 from Joseph C. Grew, Director of the Office of Far Eastern Affairs, to L. Curtis Guise in Claremont, California. Replying to Guise's letter of June 13, Grew states that the Department of State possesses no information or statistics concerning the number of American-born Japanese who divested themselves of Japanese nationality under the laws of 1916 and 1924, since such individuals were not required to report their expatriation to United States authorities. He explains that authoritative records exist solely in the archives of Japanese consular offices and government ministries in Japan, and that the Department knows of no other reliable sources.
subfiles.title: Letter from Joseph C. Grew to L. Curtis Guise on Absence of Expatriation Records
